strengths: The paper resolves significant open questions posed in the foundational work of Raman and Raman (2025), specifically regarding the relationship between noiseless non-uniform generation and non-uniform noise-dependent generation, as well as providing the first exact characterization of non-uniformly noise-dependently generatable language classes.

The collapse of the finite noise hierarchy for uniform and non-uniform generation (showing equivalence between noise level 1 and any finite noise level i >= 1) is a surprising, elegant, and insightful result, establishing a striking contrast with the infinite hierarchy established for generation in the limit by Bai et al. (2026).
The technical execution is exceptionally clean. In particular, Lemma 3.2 employs a very neat combinatorial partitioning and closure argument that yields the collapse directly.

The separation result (Theorem 2.15) uses a clean and convincing diagonal/greedy construction on column unions to show that even a single noisy string strictly restricts generation capabilities compared to the noiseless setting.
The paper is very well written, mathematically precise, self-contained, and places its results clearly within the evolving literature on language generation in the limit.
weaknesses: The study remains strictly within the idealized, non-computational/information-theoretic Gold-style language generation model; discussing the implications for computationally bounded algorithms or practical generative language modeling would further broaden the paper's reach.

The discussion could briefly elaborate on why the hierarchy collapses for uniform/non-uniform generation while remaining strict for general generation in the limit, providing more conceptual intuition beyond the technical proof of Lemma 3.2.

strengths: The paper resolves multiple open problems posed by Raman and Raman (ICML 2025), specifically establishing a complete characterization of non-uniform noise-dependent generatability and showing a strict separation between noiseless and noise-level-1 non-uniform generatability.

The central equivalence result (Theorem 2.14 / Theorem 3.3) is both surprising and elegant: while Bai et al. (SODA 2026) proved an infinite hierarchy for noise levels in the standard generation-in-the-limit model, this paper proves that for uniform and non-uniform generation, generatability with noise level 1 is equivalent to generatability with any finite noise level $i \ge 1$.

The mathematical proofs are remarkably clean and insightful. In particular, the combinatorial projection argument in Lemma 3.2 showing $NC_{i-1}(\mathcal{C}) \ge \lfloor \sqrt{NC_i(\mathcal{C})} \rfloor$ is ingenious and executed with admirable clarity.
The paper is very well-written, clearly organized, and positions itself thoroughly within the recent literature on language generation in the limit.
weaknesses: The paper focuses strictly on the theoretical paradigm of language generation in the limit (in the style of Gold / Angluin / Kleinberg-Mullainathan), which is somewhat stylized and distant from practical large language models despite the motivating remarks in the introduction.

The manuscript would benefit from a brief discussion on whether any bounds on the generation time $t^\star$ blow up as a function of the noise level $i$ when reducing noise level $i$ to noise level 1 via the contrapositive iteration of Lemma 3.2 (i.e., quantifying the rate of increase of $NC_i$ relative to $NC_1$).

strengths: The paper resolves important open problems posed by Raman & Raman (ICML 2025), specifically proving that non-uniform generation is strictly more powerful than noisy non-uniform generation, and establishing the first complete characterization of non-uniform noise-dependent generatability.

The core conceptual contribution—showing that for both uniform and non-uniform generation, generatability with a single noisy string is equivalent to generatability with any finite number of noisy strings—is surprising and provides an insightful contrast to the infinite noise hierarchy proven for generation in the limit by Bai et al. (SODA 2026).

The mathematical proofs are technically sound, elegant, and concise. In particular, the combinatorial pigeonhole argument in Lemma 3.2 relating noisy closure dimensions across noise levels is remarkably clean.
The paper is well-written, logically organized, and does an excellent job contextualizing its findings within the growing literature on language generation in the limit.
weaknesses: The work is purely theoretical within a stylized, Gold-style learning-in-the-limit framework; while it provides conceptual insights into learning from corrupted data, the direct practical implications for real-world large language models are somewhat distant.

In the proof of Theorem 2.15, the description accompanying Algorithm 1 (specifically regarding how index j is selected and how the loop advances) is slightly informal in its phrasing, though the underlying diagonalization argument is mathematically sound.
The scope of the paper is quite specialized, primarily speaking to researchers working directly on formal models of language generation.

strengths: Resolves prominent open questions in the literature: The paper resolves an open question posed by Raman & Raman (ICML 2025) by establishing a strict separation between noiseless non-uniform generation and generation with noise level 1, and by providing the first exact structural characterization for non-uniform noise-dependent generatability.

Surprising and elegant collapse result: The paper establishes that for both uniform and non-uniform generation, generatability with noise level 1 is equivalent to generatability with noise level i for any finite i >= 1 (Theorems 2.16 and 3.3). This sharply and surprisingly contrasts with the infinite hierarchy established for general generation in the limit by Bai, Panigrahi, and Zhang (SODA 2026).

High technical soundness and mathematical beauty: The core combinatorial reduction in Lemma 3.2 (bounding NC_{i-1}(C) from below by the square root of NC_i(C)) is clean, ingenious, and fully worked out with remarkable clarity.
Exceptionally clear presentation: The paper is self-contained, contextualizes all definitions and past work thoroughly, and develops proofs in a transparent, modular fashion.
weaknesses: Stylized theoretical model: As with much of the literature following Kleinberg and Mullainathan (2024), the framework is purely learning-theoretic and does not immediately translate to practical LLM training pipelines or continuous representations.

The characterization for uniform noise-dependent generation (Theorem 3.5) simplifies the characterization of Raman & Raman (2025), but is largely a direct corollary of the collapse theorem (Theorem 3.3) and existing characterizations.

strengths: The paper resolves two major open problems posed by Raman & Raman (ICML 2025): it proves that noiseless non-uniform generation is strictly more powerful than non-uniform generation with noise level 1 (separating noiseless and noisy non-uniform generation), and it provides the first exact characterization of non-uniform noise-dependent generatability.

The collapse theorem (Theorem 2.16 / Lemma 3.2), showing that uniform and non-uniform generation with noise level 1 is equivalent to generation with noise level $i$ for any finite $i \ge 1$, provides a striking and insightful contrast to the strict infinite hierarchy known for standard generation in the limit by Bai, Panigrahi, and Zhang (SODA 2026).

The mathematical arguments, particularly the combinatorial partitioning argument in Lemma 3.2 ($NC_{i-1}(C) \ge \lfloor \sqrt{NC_i(C)} \rfloor$) and the adversary construction in Theorem 2.17, are elegant, technically sound, and remarkably self-contained.
The paper is very well written and structured, presenting definitions, intuition, and formal proofs clearly and concisely.
weaknesses: The study remains purely within the abstract, idealized framework of language generation in the limit (Gold-style learning theory), meaning the connection to practical LLM training and noise robustness in modern deep learning is conceptual rather than immediately applicable.

Several foundational lemmas (e.g., Lemma 3.1 and Lemma 4.1) rely heavily on known closure-dimension and consistency techniques from prior work (LRT25, RR25), though Lemma 3.2 and Theorem 2.17 introduce substantial original technical depth.
The paper does not explore broader noise regimes, such as benign/random noise distributions or computational/sample complexity aspects of noisy generation.

strengths: Resolves open questions posed by Raman & Raman (ICML 2025), specifically by proving a strict separation between noiseless and noisy non-uniform generation, and providing a full characterization for non-uniform noise-dependent generatability.

Uncovers a surprising structural collapse: while Bai et al. (SODA 2026) established an infinite hierarchy for standard generation in the limit across noise levels, this paper establishes that for both uniform and non-uniform generation, generatability with noise level i >= 1 collapses to noise level 1.

The core technical step (Lemma 3.2) establishing NC_{i-1}(C) >= floor(sqrt(NC_i(C))) is remarkably elegant, concise, and technically sound, providing a clean combinatorial bound on the noisy closure dimension.
The paper is very well-written, clearly organized, and thoroughly situated within the recent literature on language generation in the limit.
weaknesses: The results are situated strictly within the abstract Gold-style framework of language generation in the limit; the connection to practical LLM pre-training and real-world noisy data remains purely metaphorical.

Computational complexity / computability of the constructed generator algorithms is not addressed, as the algorithms rely on non-constructive search over infinite closures and consistent language sets (though this is standard in this learning-theoretic framework).
Beyond the core arguments in Lemma 3.2 and Theorem 2.17, several proofs adapt existing characterization machinery from Raman & Raman (2025) and Li et al. (2025).
